utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in the courtroom. Mark Harmon, Salvatore Cannata, Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Mr. Perisic is represented by Novak Lukic, Tina Drolec, and any minute now Boris Zorko should enter the courtroom. He is copying the documents right now so that we can use them in our work today -- well, here he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Good morning to you, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. To remind you again to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you so much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Novakovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard the promise I gave to the Trial Chamber last night, so I would like to ask for you to bear that in mind so that we can complete it within the first session today. I don't know whether e-court is functioning now, but I would like to call P1048 if possible. If not, then we have hard copies here for everyone. This document is dated -- or, rather, it comes from the Main Staff of the SVK dated 19th of August, 1994. It is called: "Operative Report on the Situation in Western Bosnia." And, General, what I wish to cover briefly is what we can see in the lower part of this document. It says that Fikret Abdic has personally taken over the command, and then underneath would you please read to yourself what is written there. And just tell us briefly what it is that this document is about, what was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the last phase of the conflict in Western Bosnia between the forces loyal to Fikret Abdic and the forces loyal to Alija Izetbegovic. At this stage of the conflict, the forces loyal to Alija Izetbegovic are about to win, to defeat the forces loyal to Fikret Abdic. And from this request of Fikret Abdic we can see that he is asking for more ammunition and that he is getting ready to leave the territory of this autonomous region of Western Bosnia that he had proclaimed and that his only option is to pull out the people via the territory of Serbian Krajina into Croatia and then further on to the west. That was his intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that what happened after this?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened immediately within the next day or two. I had occasion to observe this. The refugees came to the Serbian territory and then moved on towards the border crossing in Turan, near Karlovci which was a town under the Croatian control. They were halted there by Croatian authorities and Croatian armed formations, and they were not allowed to pass further on into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many members of the units of Alija Izetbegovic were there as well as civilian population, according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Alija Izetbegovic's army or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I made a mistake. I apologise. I had in mind the units of Fikret Abdic and the civilians. Can you give us an approximate number of the people who crossed into the territory of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was between 25.000 and 30.000 people. That was the total number, which was greater than the population that lived in Kordun at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that LiveNote is not working, but I will continue nevertheless following transcript on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, one of the positions that you held at the time was deputy commander for security and logistics, so let me ask you from that point of view, from the point of view of security, was this situation a security risk or a security threat at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Potentially this could have been a problem, and this is why members of the people's defence of autonomous region of Western Bosnia who came to our territory were disarmed. All weapons they had were confiscated from them, so that we could take care of them in an organised manner. Temporary refugee camps were set up in order to ensure that these people were safe in the territory under our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was Serif Mustedanagic, General?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Serif Mustedanagic was the commander of the army of Fikret Abdic which was called People's Defence of the Autonomous Region of Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at P1141.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an enactment of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and then underneath we see Pauk command. The date is November 1994. And then underneath we see your signature and your name. General, let me ask you first, what was it, Pauk command, or Spider command?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pauk command consisted of two parts. One part comprised the Supreme Command of People's Defence of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia. The other part comprised a group of officers of the Serbian Army of Krajina, SVK, headed by me pursuant to an order from Mr. Martic. Our responsibility was to assist in planning of combat operations and in control or direction of combat operations. Before carrying out combat operations and following their completion, our Serbian part which consisted of four to five officers had no further responsibilities nor were they authorised to command anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now tell me, please, about the content of this document. Do you remember this? Do you remember submitting such a request? And what was the reason for it?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document hails from the period when the temporary operations group Pauk was established and based on what Mr. Fikret Abdic agreed on in Belgrade, and he told me that he had agreed with Mr. Milosevic and with Mr. Karadzic based on which some financial assistance had been promised to him. This financial assistance was provided by the SVK and it consisted mostly of equipment and ammunition. And what the SVK didn't have itself, as you can see from this request, I tried to obtain from the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with this document. How long was this Pauk command in operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pauk command existed until the 5th of August, 1995, that's how long it was in operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this is the time when the Operation Storm, Croatian Operation Storm, began? I apologise --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise for formulating my question in this manner. Did -- we saw the document, and after August of 1994 were the forces of Fikret Abdic active at all? Did they try to regain their territory; and if so, did they have any success in that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late 1994 after a grave humanitarian situation which existed, these forces attempted to regain their territory by force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. -- Mr. Novakovic told us that Pauk command existed until the 5th of August, 1995. And then you asked after August 1994. Was it August 1994 you meant or did you mean August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant 1994 because we were dealing with the document which provided information that the forces of Alija Izetbegovic would push them out of that territory. So from that time on for the following year, that's the period I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have finished with this topic, and the next issue that I'm interested in is something that we have touched upon yesterday. So the next document that I would like us to look at is from the Defence 65 ter list 00748D, which is a decision on uniting RSK and Republika Srpska dated the 20th of May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the year. Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the year. They heard up to the 20th of May. I don't know what year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, yesterday at the end of your evidence we touched upon the relationship that existed between Martic and Karadzic, and during your proofing I showed you this document. So I'm asking you now, do you know something about this decision, do you know what was the political background to this decision, and what was Milosevic's reaction to this decision at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this was the third instance since 1992 that such a decision was being passed on uniting Republika Srpska and RSK. This decision was adopted based on very similar political views of Mr. Martic and Mr. Karadzic, and Mr. Milosevic believed this to be a provocation addressed to the international community because they -- there had already existed two internationally recognised states: Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. And in their territories they tried to create something that was unacceptable for the international community, a state -- a new state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now admit this into evidence, Your Honours, this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D443.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned something yesterday and I would like to develop it further; namely, your participation in negotiations in Geneva. Would you please tell us what negotiations those were and who participated in them.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These negotiations were planned and were held on the 3rd of August, 1995. Mr. Stoltenberg headed the negotiations. On the Croatian side there were Mr. Pasalic and Madam Skare Ozbolt, General Stipetic, Admiral Domazet, and on our side I was the one who headed the delegation comprising another three persons Mr. Macura, Mr. Prijic, and Mr. Vojnovic. On the Croatian side those were fake negotiations and we knew that ahead of time. Their intention was to present their requests which we in turn would reject, and then they would have a basis for international recognition and acceptance of the aggression. We knew that this was their position before we went to Geneva, and I'm saying this for the first time here, that this is something that Mr. Stoltenberg very honestly admitted to me in Geneva during negotiations. After --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us go step by step. What did Mr. Stoltenberg tell you and what situation during those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially negotiations were conducted in such a manner where international intermediaries would hold several talks with both delegations, that of the Republic of Croatia, those -- that of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I was informed by Mr. Stoltenberg, as the chief of the delegation, that the Croats were insisting on holding a joint plenary session. Mr. Stoltenberg said to me then that they - meaning the international mediators - will draft a proposed agreement that would be supposed to be accepted as a result of those negotiations. He thought it would be the most useful thing for our side, for their paper or their draft created by international intermediaries for us to accept it in its entirety, including the acceptance of the then-still-contentious plan labelled Z-4. After consultations with my delegation members, I decided to go along with that proposal. At the plenary session which ensued, if you wish me to explain this, the Croatian side came up with a torrent of abuse and they sought that we raise our hands, sign unconditional capitulation, they wanted all of us in the RSK to be tried as war criminals, et cetera. I was the only one who spoke on behalf of my delegation, and I said that I don't want to use such vocabulary and such term of voice. I stated that the Serbian delegation was supporting in its entirety the international mediators' proposal of the agreement, and I repeated that after the negotiations in front of 70, 80 international journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction when you said that you accepted the proposal coming from the international community?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian side up-to-date has ignored this fact, and they don't even want to mention it. Their interpretation was and has been that they reject -- that we rejected their proposal, but the fact is that the Serbian side never even expressed their opinion of their proposal; rather, the Serbian side accepted the proposal coming from the international community, international mediators, in its entirety which includes the Z-4 Plan. And in the paper that was put forward by international mediators, that contained the dates and issues for the next subsequent meeting and negotiations, and the date was - if I remember correctly - the 10th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 9, line 15, I asked what was the reaction of the Croatian side, and you see the answer goes in that direction. What was the reaction of Mr. Stoltenberg and the international mediators when you accepted their proposal?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The international observers, Mr. Stoltenberg, Ambassador Volebaek, Ambassador Arhens, General de Lapresle, greeted and hailed my decision, but probably because of knowing what was to come and after what the Croats said. After the end of those negotiations, in my opinion they were very worried and this is the atmosphere that we parted ways in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the names. They are not well --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stoltenberg, Ambassador Geert Arhens, Ambassador Volebaek, General de Lapresle, Belgian Brigade General Peters, maybe Petars, but maybe Peters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That would be enough. In deciding to accept the international mediators' proposal, did you consult anybody else except those in your delegation before you took the decision?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consulted only with my delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next day general Croatian offensive ensued against the UN protected area, and as we saw it an aggression against the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Our delegation was not allowed to return the same day. We were allowed only around midday on the 4th of August and the attack started in the morning hours of the 4th of August. So our delegation only in the afternoon on the 4th of August landed at Belgrade airport in a UN aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, in a couple of words, tell us - although I know that you can speak volumes about that - what did you do after that and what were you active in in the subsequent period?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I departed towards Krajina from Belgrade immediately. It took me all night because the roads were congested. I could see that there were many refugees on the roads and what was the strangest in my opinion was that I saw that the Serbian settlements that I passed along the way were under intense artillery and missile fire of the Croatian forces. Also, I found a dispatch from Knin, which was one of the last ones, that I was appointed deputy commander for Kordun and Banija. Probably it was expected that the communication between Knin and the northern parts would be severed, which eventually did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who appointed you to that post?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mrksic, the then-commander of the SVK. That was his dispatch that reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and for how long?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communication with Banija was severed on that day as well, and from then on we were cut off. Croatian forces connected on the flanks of the Kordun corridor with Alija Izetbegovic's forces in Lika and drew closer to Alija Izetbegovic's forces in Western Bosnia through Banija. I had to organise the defence at Kordun; we were successful in that. Until the 6th of August, Sunday evening, we did not budge to the Croatian forces. Chaos ensued. Only when refugees from Lika entered our area and thus blocked and congested all communications and roads. After that on the 6th in the evening, together with the commander of the corps, Chief of Staff of the corps, minister of the interior of the RSK who was there, and people from police at their initiative I took a decision to try to break through towards Dvor Na Uni and that -- a part of our forces effected that breakthrough, despite the fact that the Croatian forces had cut off the road at Glina. The fight followed until the 10th, and I fought there as a common soldier with a rifle in my hand. On that Sunday I contacted General Janvier, commander of the UNPROFOR on several occasions, and this is the first time that I disclosed this. As opposed to Generals Cot and General de Lapresle, General Janvier seemed completely confused and lost out at sea. When I demanded that he protect the columns of refugees on the road and to threaten the Croatian forces with NATO aviation and air-strikes if they were to shoot at the refugees, General Janvier kept saying, "General, please, General, please, make sure that my soldiers are safe." I told General Janvier, "Mr. General, your soldiers would be the safest if they were left at home. Why did you bring them here? Why would their safety be the most important thing? Why don't you protect the people in that area," but to no avail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did combat operations last or your activities in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat activities on the road between the town of Glina and the river of Una, Dvor Na Uni, and Novi Grad and the bridge over the Una towards the territory -- Serb-controlled territory of the Republika Srpska, with the goal of defending the people on the road because we had nothing else to defend, they lasted until the 10th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, what happened with the RSK after the 10th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The briefest possible answer: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did it continue to persist as a political reality? I'd like you to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not even what has been written in Croatia's constitutional law about two autonomous districts in the territory of Croatia has not been abided by in those areas where Serbs were a majority. This has not been implemented up-to-date. Those areas are empty, destroyed, including - if I may make a personal note - the house and farm of my parents who suffered the same fate back in 1941 and then in 1995, where everything was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened to the SVK after the 10th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who, where, or when decided or made arrangements for members of the SVK immediately upon entering the territory of the RS to be disarmed. I saw that and it felt ugly, as if they were entering enemy or alien territory. I don't know why such decision was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the SVK continue to exist, the Main Staff, corps, did they exist after August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the 11th Corps continued existing -- in existence in the eastern-most part of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me revisit another topic before the final part that I could not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does the 11th Corps still exist to date or when did it come to its end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in -- during 1995 negotiations started on peaceful reintegration of that territory into the territory of the newly established Croatian state. That process was completed in a way that those areas were integrated or reintegrated into the territory of the newly established Croatian state, which meant the end of the 11th Corps. What happened to their weapons, I don't know. I wasn't in the loop. I simply have no way of knowing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When did the life of the 11th Corps come to an end? Are you able to give a date, a month, a year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the corps still existed in 1995. I know that with some degree of reliability, but in 1996 it no longer existed. I cannot remember precisely the elements of those -- this agreement. There were stages, and if I were to try to be specific I would be speculating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we adduce it under different numbers. This is the Law on the SVK which has been adduced only in parts as opposed to the Law on the VJ and the VRS; although, I tried to have it admitted in its entirety. That would be D170. Let us take a look at an article which is part of that exhibit, and then another article which has not been tendered, which has not been given an exhibit number but is important from our purposes and I believe it should be commented upon by the witness. We have provided a draft translation of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have made a speech here which I don't understand, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Law on the Serbian Army of Krajina is a voluminous document, just like the other two laws; it has over 300 articles. The Law on the Army of Yugoslavia and the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska were tendered into evidence in their entirety; whereas, the Law on the Serbian Army of Krajina was unfortunately tendered into evidence only in a limited manner, only some articles were admitted. And now I will comment with the witness on some articles which are already in evidence as part of D170, and then I want to look at some other articles which have not yet been admitted and I will -- it is quite unfortunate in my view that they have not been admitted, and I will ask that they be admitted eventually and joined with D170.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you are quite familiar with this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying this law is D170? This document is D170 that we've just got?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is D170, except for the additional articles that I will mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we see that this law was adopted on the 22nd of April, 1993. At that time you had already been commander of the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at Article 320, which are transitional provisions and final provisions at the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised that in e-court this document appears as D85, not 170.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, D85 is just this one article and D170 are other articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Article 320 is D85?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see that, General, do you have Article 320 before you?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you go on with the General, I'm also trying to find out where you find it in this document that you have given us that it was adopted on the 22nd of April, 1993, because that's what you proposed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, please. I can see the B/C/S version very clearly, but I don't know whether the same is true for you. Because the B/C/S version has the date in the heading.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask that the ELMO -- that -- be focused a bit more because we can't read the text on the ELMO. Could that be corrected, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have a problem with the system here. I'm not quite sure whether the ELMO can work, Madam Interpreter. Okay. Yeah. It's faded, I can't see either, and unfortunately you don't have the hard copy. I can guarantee you, Mr. Lukic, that on the English copy that I have there is no date. The question is: Are we looking at the same document in the English and B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please look at the heading of the document. I'm trying to cover it as quickly as possible. It says Law on the Army of the Serbian Army of Krajina, Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbian Krajina 2/1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see that, but there's no date, there's no 22nd of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, please. Now, if we were to put the B/C/S version on the ELMO, would that be of assistance to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, it would not be of assistance to me because I'm not sure whether we are looking at the same document. If your B/C/S document has a date, my English document must have a date. We must look at the same thing. The question is: Has -- are we looking at the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was translated into English were just excerpts from the document, not the document in it entirety, because the CLSS has refused to translate the entire document and only certain articles were translated. And this is how we proceeded with Witness Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, what is on the ELMO right now I do have, but there is no date there. You see, my problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- my problem is that when you make introductory remarks before you put your question, you put statements which we are not able to verify from the document. You've suggested to the witness that this document is dated the 22nd of April, 1993. We don't see that date on this document. Now, shall we accept that as correct or not? Now, rather just don't prefix your questions. Show the witness the document and start asking your questions. That avoids, one, leading; two, giving information that is unverifiable, like you've just done. Okay. Put your questions. Now we accept that you are talking about the Law on the Serbian Army of Krajina, Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbian Krajina number 2 of 1993. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I apologise. I apologise to the Chamber. This was something that was evident for me in the B/C/S version, and I had no idea that it was missing in the English version. General, can you see based on the document in front of you when this law was adopted?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On each page of this document in the Serbian it says: "Thursday, 22nd April, 1993," which is - as far as I can remember -- I know it was April. I can't claim that it was on the 22nd precisely that this law was adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to have to mark this for identification until we have the correct translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I was going to suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 320, General, says: "On the date of entry into force of this law, active officers and active junior officers of the Army of Yugoslavia who, in addition to the citizenship of the RSK, are also citizens of another Serbian state and have been appointed to duty in the Serbian Army of Krajina (hereinafter SVK) are hereby transferred into professional officers and professional non-commissioned officers of the SVK in the rank they held on the day this law entered into force." General, when did you become a member of the Serbian Army of Krajina, the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: De facto, I became a member of that army the day SVK was established. At that time we still did not have the Law on the Army and the Law on Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's now look at Article 324.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a draft translation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Professional active officers, junior officers, and military clerks of the Army of Yugoslavia, as well as civilians in -- serving in the Army of Yugoslavia who do not accept to be transferred into SVK as professional officers, professional non-commissioned officers, or civilians serving in the SVK, shall have their service terminated within 30 days from the day this law enters into force." I'm just interested in this particular paragraph of this article. Did you have any situations where you had somebody there who considered themselves a member of the VJ and were serving in the SVK and could you command such people?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This pertains exclusively to dealing with those who left the SVK and were no longer in the SVK, and logically they could not be considered members of the SVK any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to avoid any potential problems, I will ask for official translation of both of these articles, of both of these pages, and then I would ask that that official translation replace the draft translation and that these two articles be added to the existing exhibit. I think that this is technically the most viable solution. For the time being we can keep the existing exhibit number and indication of MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll add it to D85, and we'll make a note that this part is marked for identification. Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, on the first day of your evidence when we discussed your career and we saw how you were retired and what entry was made concerning your retirement, you gave answers to His Honour Moloto about the factual and formal date of your retirement, so I will now deal with that. In that document that we saw, which is your personnel file, OTP exhibit, it says that you were retired on the 30th of December, 1994, by way of the decree of -- presidential decree. And you told us that factually you retired only the 17th of October, 1995, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was then that I was informed that I had been retired. Both dates that you said are correct, and also please look at the date when I was appointed chief of the infantry administration. They antedated my retirement date subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 14th of December?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this now: Who told you this, who talked to you, and what did they talk to you about concerning your retirement?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you alone there or was there somebody else present?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mrksic, the then-commander of SVK and the last commander of SVK; General Bjelanovic, who was assistant for logistics; and myself. The three of us were together with General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did General Perisic tell you at the time, whose decision was it and what kind of a decision it was?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic said that that was the decision of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when it comes to the date of your retirement, what did he tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the date of retirement had to be what it was because in late 1994 Article 107 of the Law on the Army became invalid [as interpreted], and that article enabled servicemen to retire based on their years of service and their age.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, how did you accept this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took it well in the sense that I wanted all of this to be done and over with because I no longer had any intention of serving in anyone's army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did you no longer want to serve in anyone's army?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, after everything that had happened and the way it had happened, I no longer wanted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you signed any documents on the basis of that decision, and were you aware then that the official date of your retirement would be the 30th of December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They told me then that the Supreme Defence Council, guided by such a possibility provided by the legislation, made that decision and that that decision pertained to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, were you aware at the time, did you know that there was some sort of a negative attitude to you as officers of the SVK and the fall of the SVK among the general public and among the leadership and among the authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was well-known, and the case of us three generals -- the three of us knew that. We knew that in the top echelons of the state at the time existed a negative attitude towards us and that General Perisic shared that view as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know why, why did the political leadership and military leadership have this negative attitude towards you?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public in -- were revolted over what had happened and how it happened in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. It was our understanding that the state and the military leadership at the time was the best option for the FRY at the time, and in that option the officers and then the other leadership in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina could be blamed for everything. General Perisic even mentioned something like that in his conversation with us three generals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I make an intervention here. Madam Interpreter, I thought you moved away from the mike and you didn't tell us where this public revolted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The public in Serbia, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not understand your answer, Mr. Novakovic. You say: "It was our understanding that the state and the military leadership at the time was the best option ..." How can -- what do you mean the state is the best option and the leadership -- "... was the best option for the FRY at the time, and in that option the officers and then the other leadership in the Republic of Serbian Krajina could be blamed for everything." I really don't understand what that sentence is saying, unless you have been misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I said was that for the state and military leadership at the time of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in order to preserve their position of power, the best option in terms of the revolt of the population was the -- was to blame us from the Republic of -- from the Serbian Republic of the Krajina for everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That makes better sense. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the position of the political and the military leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in terms of the security of the FRY and in terms of what happened with the exodus of the Serbs from the Krajina, particularly the Serbian -- the Army of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you asking me when you're talking about security are you talking about internal security situation or some kind of external danger?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To be more precise, I'm talking about internal security situation and the political situation.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know - and this has not been disproved by anything to date - there was a concern that, first of all, dissatisfied Serbs from the Krajina who were refugees at the time could, in an uncontrolled outburst of dissatisfaction, turn to some kind of expression that would no longer be possible to control. To tell you the truth, I believe that perhaps I myself contributed to that to a degree when I saw before going to Geneva a kind of nonchalant attitude. I did state a sentence in Belgrade in the sense of, "You just keep on playing if here in the Nemanja and Kneza Milosa Street where these main institutions of the state are located find themselves surrounded by 300 [as interpreted] people from the Krajina, the space will be quite small and tight for everybody, and then later when the column of refugees started no one could enter Belgrade." But General Mrksic or I were not able to cross the Drina itself to enter either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said 300.000, this is page 24, line 23.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I said 300.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And does that quote end at the end of the sentence, "... but General Mrksic and I were not able to cross the Drina itself to enter either." Is that where your quotation ends? I thought you were quoting something. The stenographer start here: "I did state a sentence in Belgrade in the sense of, "You just keep on playing if here in the Nemanja and Kneza Milosa Street where the main institutions of the state are located to find themselves surrounded by 300.000 people from the Krajina, the space will be quite small and tight for everybody, and then later when the column of refugees started no one could enter Belgrade." Is that what you say you said in Belgrade and is that where you end? Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The quotation ends with that, and I also said later that refugees could not enter Belgrade later and that General Mrksic and I were also stopped from entering Serbia over the Drina River, which is the official boundary entering into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And where were you in the meantime, after the 10th of August until this conversation with General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 10th of August until the 23rd of September, I was in Republika Srpska, in Prijedor and Banja Luka. And then I crossed into Serbia incognito. From that time until the 17th of October I was in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I'm only going to have a couple more questions and I'm sure I will make you happy when I tell you that I have almost finished with my examination. I'm sure everybody in the courtroom will also be relieved. General, we spoke about the meetings that you had with General Perisic, with Milosevic, and we also saw that General Mladic was present sometimes. Judge Moloto asked you yesterday, I think, about the levels of the top professional officer of an army. At one point in time you were the commander of the Serbian Army of the Krajina; General Mladic was the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska; and General Perisic was the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. What I would like to know particularly is this: At that level, based on what you know about the events, General Mladic -- was General Perisic an authority to him? Did he have any kind of a subordinated relationship to him and did that perhaps also apply to you?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally, no, of course not. General Perisic, first of all let's clarify that, did not have any kind of formally superior position in relation to General Mladic. Informally, the case was even less so; it wasn't the case at all. Because General Mladic is a man who believes in his knowledge and in his ability. At the time he was in touch with foreign ministers, foreign generals, from Greece, Russia, UNPROFOR generals, in contact with ambassadors. The questions that needed to be resolved in Yugoslavia he would resolve with Mr. Milosevic. So generally at that point in time as far as he was concerned, General Perisic was an audience that at some points was supposed to provide him with resources. As far as I'm concerned, just like Mr. Mladic, I was at this function before General Perisic took on the duty of the Chief of Staff of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. So my fate did not depend on General Perisic. Very quickly I realised that as far as I was concerned General Perisic was not an important address in Belgrade for me. Everything that had to be done was really not referred to General Perisic. If I were to exaggerate I could say that he wasn't to be asked about anything. Perhaps that wasn't quite true, but basically none of the decisions were under his authority or jurisdiction. I found this out in the following way. The supreme political and military authority was in the hands of Mr. Milosevic. If the army was supposed to resolve something then he would call his man from his political party, Mr. Lilic, who could possibly have a say in this. He could possibly tell General Perisic something in the sense that some decision would need to be implemented. To tell you the truth, throughout the whole time that I was the commander of the Serbian Army of the Krajina, it was my sense that politicians have some kind of base or foundation in Belgrade. Policemen had some kind of base in Belgrade, but my company, the one that I should be relying on in Belgrade, it was the least important one. I realised I had no base to lean on in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "my firm, my company," you're thinking of the Army of the Serbian Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's leading, Your Honour. I object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you're saying "police," you're also saying police of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. That's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it was not translated correctly into the English, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who were you thinking of when you said "our politicians" and "our policemen"?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking about the situation during the time that I was the commander of the Serbian Army of the Krajina, it is clear that I meant - and I confirm that now - the politicians and the policemen from the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, for whom I said that they were looking for some kind of backing in Belgrade, when the General Staff was a body that provided the least backing as far as we were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I have finished my examination-in-chief, and I thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to make everything quite clear, when you say "the General Staff was a body that provided the least backing as far as we were concerned," what General Staff are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you too, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have P177 on the monitor. I'm referring to English e-court translation 06117595, page 4 in the English and the B/C/S page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What we'll be looking at in just a moment, General Novakovic, is your personnel file. It's P1777.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I need the next -- that is not the page I'm looking for in English. Let me -- it should be page 4 in the English. All right. That's the correct page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I'm interested in examining with you just briefly, and very briefly, General Novakovic, is your career trajectory as reflected in your official personnel file. And I'd like to focus your attention on -- the first entry I'd call your attention to is the entry that -- wherein you are assigned as command of the 5th VO Zagreb garrison as the assistant chief of training. Do you see that entry? It is the third one from -- should be the third one from the bottom in the English on the right-hand side? Do you see that entry, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, is that the entry where it says: Assistant chief training department of organ for operational and training activities, command of the 5th Military District Zagreb garrison?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And that was -- you were assigned, were you, to Zagreb, in Croatia, pursuant to an order of the SSNO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order of the SSNO because it went for an appointment to a post of a colonel as per establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Then following that you were temporarily assigned to work in the 5th Military District, 1st Operations Group, and that was pursuant to -- it says NPU of the SSNO. Can you tell us what the acronym NPU stands for?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, that would be the last row or the last column. This is the Chief of Personnel Administration of the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, where were you stationed when you were assigned to the 5th Military District, 1st Operations Group, was that still in Zagreb or was that elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I was not in Zagreb. I was seconded to the war college, College for People's Defence, in Belgrade pursuant to a special order on -- to that effect which was not entered here. And in the centre of high military schools, I was told about this order of the Chief of the Personnel Administration of the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence where I'm deployed in the command of the operations group 1 which was then being established in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And your next entry reflects that you were assigned to the 1st Operations Group, the 4th Partisan Brigade in Vrginmost. And who ordered you to that assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused by this entry, Mr. Harmon, because at that time I was not a brigade commander. The brigade commander, as I've already stated here, Lieutenant-Colonel Mladenovic who previously had been in the Karlovac garrison which was the domicile garrison of the aforementioned 4th Partisan Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm interested in is the last entry on the page that reflects an assignment to the 1st Operations Group, 4th Partisan Brigade in Vrginmost. Did you receive such an assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assigned to that post on the 18th of May, 1992, when the Yugoslav People's Army - and then Lieutenant-Colonel Mladenovic who hailed from Serbia - withdrew to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this entry in your personnel file that reflects the assignment date being -- the order date being the 28th of October, 1991, is that correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say because I never saw that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. And at the time you received that order you were in the JNA, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received this order, Mr. Harmon, because -- because my superior command was -- well, the superior command to the command of the 1st Operations Group was the command which previously had been in Zagreb, and that was the command of the north-west front line and theatre, which then went to Sarajevo and subsequently there occurred those events in Dobrovoljacka Street, but I've never seen this order issued by the SSNO and I've never acted upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever go to the 1st Operations Group, the 4th Partisan Brigade, in Vrginmost? And that calls for a yes or no answer?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the 1st Operations Group, that's one thing. But I repeat, I went to the command of the 4th Partisan Brigade on the 18th of May, 1992, after the JNA had withdrawn and after there was no command of Operations Group 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you went to the 1st Operations Group, were you a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if we could turn the page in English. I'd like to look at the next entry in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This entry says: "Assigned to TO of the SAO of Krajina to the STO," which means territorial defence staff, "of the 3rd Banija-Kordun operations zone in Glina." Did you assume that particular position?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, instead of the command of the operations Group 1, there was established one operations group for Kordun and another operations group for Banija instead of the command of the Operations Group 1 which was in charge of Kordun and Banija both. I was in charge of the operations group for Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And at the time you assumed that position were you a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this entry reflects that this was pursuant to an order. It says "NPU." What does NPU stand for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think I did ask that, Your Honour. I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It says pursuant to the NPU of the SSNO, and it gives a number and a date. Did you receive a copy of that order?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And so how was it you moved from the operations group in Belgrade to the Krajina as a JNA officer without an order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness's answer was not that he was in operations group in Belgrade. I believe that Mr. Harmon has misinterpreted the witness's answer given previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understood --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Maybe I understood, General -- but let's clarify this point right now. Were you in an operations group -- were you assigned in Belgrade before you went to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I was sent for schooling to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Then my question -- I maintain my question. How was it you went from schooling in Belgrade to the Krajina without receiving an order from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you get that from. I did not say that. I stated that I received that order. I don't believe we should skip from one order to another and create confusion. So the order stating temporarily seconded to the 5th Military District of the 1st Operations Group, no garrison assignment, chief of personnel administration of the SSNO, 24-286, 27th September, 1991, that order was given to me while I was in Belgrade in military school by Mr. -- General Koturovic, and this means that I did not go to Krajina without an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then we understand each other. You did go to the Krajina pursuant to an order of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the entry that states that you were assigned for the purpose of representation to the MUP of the Government of the RSK to the formation of the special police unit, Vojnic garrison. Was that -- at the time you -- did you assume that position?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the time you assumed that position, were you a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. The JNA still existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you -- were you assigned to that position pursuant to the order that is reflected in the right-hand column of this entry?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I do not recall that order specifically, but I believe that this was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now you've told us in your direct examination about the next two entries, and I won't go into those two entries. You see the two entries I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we continue in your personnel file, sir, we then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn the page in the -- both the B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the next entry that appears in your personnel file is the entry that relates to your termination -- your retroactive termination from the VJ on -- in December of 1994. Can you -- having looked at this personnel file, is there any reflection in your personnel file, in this portion of your personnel file, that shows that when you accepted duties at the SVK you terminated your service in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my duty, Mr. Harmon, it is true that I terminated my service in the Army of Yugoslavia. However, I maintained the status of an officer of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So in the personnel file there is no reflection that you terminated your service from the VJ, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Harmon, shall we go back to the previous or preceding page?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could assist the witness and go back to the preceding page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you show me on this page where it is that you terminated your service in the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The penultimate entry in the Serbian language, it states here -- it's -- he's deployed to the 1st Army, garrison not yet determined, dated 30th of May, 1992. Mr. Harmon, in reality there must exist a document that I saw with Mr. Lukic where I declare and sign that I stay in the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. This is not recorded here in those entries, and this reference, deployed to the 1st Army, garrison not yet determined, refers to the offer to those who stayed in the Territorial Defence of the RSK in order to regulate the housing issues. The very fact that the garrison has not yet been determined means that I was not assigned a duty in the Army of Yugoslavia. And the last entry on this page in the Serbian language, I've already commented upon it in my previous testimony. By a decree of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, at one point I did at the request of Mr. Martic get an appointment to the General Staff of the VJ to the post of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- head or chief of the infantry administration --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- let me interrupt you. My question to you was: Where is it reflected in your personnel file that you terminated your service in the VJ prior to the entry that shows you were retroactively retired?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the very fact that in this personnel file you can find the duty that I was assigned to confirm what I've been stating, and which is true, that I did not hold any post in the VJ. I reiterate, I maintained the status of an officer in the VJ after having the status of an officer of the JNA, but I held no duty in the Army of Yugoslavia, apart from this one that I tried to tell you about but you interrupted me, which I never assumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it, sir, that we are in agreement then that your personnel file does not reflect that you terminated your service in the VJ? Now, you testified earlier, General Novakovic, about Article 107 of the Law on the VJ, which deals specifically with termination from professional military service. And one of the bases of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic is standing so I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not recall that at any point General Novakovic testified about Article 107 of the VJ act. I have not shown it to him. If Mr. Harmon were to broach that subject, it would be useful to have this document placed in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He did discuss Article 107 this morning. He said that General Perisic told him at the -- when he had a conversation with General Perisic that Article 107 was invalid. I think that's on page 22 or 23 of this morning's transcript. I'm happy to place Article -- if we could have P197 put on the screen, please. And the reference to Article 107 was page 21, line 23. If we could turn to Article 107 in this document. It's page 25 of the English, and in the Serbian language -- just a moment, please. Page 9. The English is on page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, this is the Law on the Army. It is Article 107 of the Law on the Army, and it indicates under what circumstances a professional military officer or non-commissioned officer shall be terminated. And you can see a number of sub-points, 1 through 6, and you can see thereafter it -- that it -- there is also a reference to military service being terminated when there are 30 years of pensionable service, years of service, and if the needs of the service so require, and et cetera. So my question, sir, is: Did you terminate your service in the VJ at your own request when you started your service in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have an occasion to send a personal request. Rather, as I stated, I was told that the Supreme Council decided that the three generals, the three of us, be pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, you've misunderstood my question. My question was: Before you were retroactively retired and at any time prior to or during your service in the SVK, did you voluntarily terminate your service in the VJ, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, if under service in the VJ you mean formally maintaining the status of an officer of the VJ, then I can tell you that I sent no such request ever. However, if under service in the VJ you mean also performing a duty and existing within the forces of the VJ in the organic sense, then it was not the case [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while you were serving in the SVK, General Novakovic, what remuneration did you receive from the authorities in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think on page 38, line 10, it says "then it was not the case," and I think it's a wrong translation. I think the witness said something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, can you remember your answer and can you repeat your answer, please. You said: "However, if under the service in the VJ you mean ... performing a duty ..." Can you complete that sentence for us, please, because there may be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Performing a duty or being a part of the VJ in the organic sense, then it is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now can we continue with the question I asked you. Can you tell us, sir, while you were serving in the SVK what remuneration you received from the RSK for your services?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who paid your salary?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can call it a salary, then it came from the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who paid your pension and who continues to pay your pension?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nowadays, it is the Republic of Serbia. However, Mr. Harmon, I think we're skipping over some important matters by your leave --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask the questions. And if you need to explain something -- but my questions I think are fairly clear and concrete. Who paid your pension? I'll ask you a slightly different question. Who paid your pension after you were retroactively retired?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do they continue to pay your pension to this day?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no longer. Nowadays it is the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were serving in the SVK, who paid your medical benefits and insurance?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like other former officers of the Yugoslav People's Army who maintained their status within the VJ were paid -- had their medical insurance through the Ministry of Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I think that it came under their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And who resolved your housing issues? Who was in charge of your housing?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, my housing was provided only in January of last year, something to what I was entitled to. My suffering, if I can say so, lasted for a long time and I had to move nine times within that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And so -- do I understand you to say that you received no housing benefits from the date of your retroactive retirement until last year from any governmental source of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Harmon. That is not true. Until January of last year I did not have housing. During that time I received certain compensation specified by legislation because my housing had not been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, General. Who provided you with those compensations?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia, whose citizen I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday we touched upon the topic of your salary, and you testified you didn't care much about the salary you were receiving. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I remember it very well, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, while you were serving in the SVK, did you receive additional compensation in addition to your normal salary?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was an amount paid for serving in hardship circumstances, whether it was paid to us at that time or retroactively I really couldn't tell you right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have P177 [sic] on the monitor, and I'm -- would like English -- e-court English translation 06117677 ET and the B/C/S page 86 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 177 you want or 1777?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I thought I said -- I made a special effort to say three 7s, Your Honour. Apparently I didn't. I failed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Both occasions you failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I failed. Triple 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, before you is a decision dated the 10th of February, 1994. Can you take a look at that, sir, and does this refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure that I have ever seen this and that this was ever given to me. If this was indeed drawn up, it was drawn up for the personnel centre. I don't remember seeing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, this is a document, sir, that grants you additional compensation for service under difficult or special conditions, and that means during the period of time that you were serving in the SVK. Do you remember receiving that additional compensation over and above your salary?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, Mr. Harmon, and I don't see that this was indeed decided that way here. Do -- you see here basic salary and then blank times factor. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, let me direct your attention -- let me direct your attention to sub-part (C) of -- it looks to me like it is about a third of the way down the page and it says that you were granted additional compensation in the amount of 4 per cent of the basic salary. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that. It says 4, but what this figure 4 is about, I don't know. If it's 4 per cent of the basic salary -- then when you see what the salary was, then you can calculate what 4 per cent of that salary it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Let's see if we can make it larger for you to see, and -- is that better for you to see now, sir? We can -- can you read that, sir? If you're having difficulties, sir, let me give you a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you're having difficulty, I can provide you with a hard copy of this document, sir. It might assist you in reading it.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see. Yes. This is percentage. Under (C) after figure 4 it says per cent. That's what it looks like to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I'm finished with that document. Sir, in addition to that compensation did you apply on the 19th of December, 2000, for the VJ to compensate you for unused annual leave which you had not taken in 1991, 1992, 1993, and 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, Mr. Harmon. I followed suit after a number of officers did it, inquiring why I hadn't done it myself. This is when I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And could I have P1880 on the monitor, please. I'm not seeing the B/C/S version on the stand -- on the monitor. So again I have a hard copy. I can provide this to the witness. I'm sorry. If we could have page 23 of the B/C/S then it will appear on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, can you read that? Otherwise I have a hard copy. I can provide you with a hard copy. It might make it easier for you to read. With the assistance of the usher --

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we scroll up on the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, sir, have you had a chance to look at that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you receive a copy of that decision, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received it from Colonel Begovic. I know him personally and this decision was given to me and they acted upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that document, sir. I want to focus on your retroactive retirement. You told us today that there was a sentiment that was against you from the highest political and military levels as a result of the loss of the Krajina. That's how I understood your testimony. Did I understand it correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the period after August 1995, then yes that's correct. That's the period I had in mind in my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were you and the other generals, General Bjelanovic, General Mrksic, and General Celeketic considered responsible in some -- in the eyes of the political establishment and the military establishment for the loss of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me whether political and military establishment of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia considered us responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's what I was asking you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. You testified that you were informed that there was a decision of the Supreme Defence Council that you were to be retroactively retired. Did you see a copy of that decision or that session of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the decision of the Supreme Defence Council then. They handed me the presidential decree of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Lilic, which I have in my possession to this day, as well as the decision of the personnel administration which was drafted pursuant to the presidential decree. Both of these documents pertain to my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we have P766 under seal, so we'll have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we have -- and I would like to have English page 2 and B/C/S page 2 on the monitor, please. I can give the witness a hard copy. It might be of assistance to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need it, Mr. Harmon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, this, sir, what is before you are the minutes of the 45th Session of the Supreme Defence Council that was held on the 5th of October, 1995. And if you kindly read that, and then when you get to the bottom of the page in your language would you let me know and we can turn the page and we can see the remaining text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm directing Your Honours obviously to item 3. Could we turn to the next page in the Serbian language version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you read that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I have page 3 rather than item 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And item 3 was previously on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have -- I'd given you an opportunity to read, sir. It appears to be item 3. It's the highlighted portion in yellow. Have you read the highlighted portion in yellow? That was the portion I wanted to direct your attention to.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's on this page, yes, item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Now, this is the document that generated your retroactive retirement. This reflects the debate and the discussion and the decisions that led to your retroactive retirement. Now, I'm interested in your comments on this text.

utterances.speaker: MILE NOVAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat what I stated earlier today, and that is that it seemed to me that the then-state and military leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia thought that it was most convenient to blame us entirely for the fall of Krajina. I do not want to pardon myself or anybody else for what had happened. And this is why they passed this decision. To tell you the truth, I don't know what other decision they could have made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can go into public session, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.
